/*

Chapter 7.  It is not written to be comprehensible without the
explanation in that book.

Written by Joseph O'Rourke.

redistributed in its entirety provided that this copyright notice is
not removed.

*/
#include        <stdio.h>
#include        <math.h>
#define EXIT_SUCCESS 0
#define EXIT_FAILURE 1
#define X       0
#define Y       1
typedef enum { FALSE, TRUE } bool;
typedef enum { Pin, Qin, Unknown } tInFlag;

#define DIM     2               /* Dimension of points */
typedef int     tPointi[DIM];   /* type integer point */
typedef double  tPointd[DIM];   /* type double point */
#define PMAX    1000            /* Max # of pts in polygon */

typedef tPointi tPolygoni[PMAX];/* type integer polygon */

/*---------------------------------------------------------------------
Function prototypes.
---------------------------------------------------------------------*/
void    ClosePostscript( void );
void	PrintSharedSeg( tPointd p, tPointd q );
double  Dot( tPointi a, tPointi b );
int	AreaSign( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c );
char    SegSegInt( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c, tPointi d, tPointd p, tPointd q );
char    ParallelInt( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c, tPointi d, tPointd p, tPointd q );
bool    Between( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c );
void    Assigndi( tPointd p, tPointi a );
void    SubVec( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c );
bool    LeftOn( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c );
bool    Left( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c );
void    PrintPoly( int n, tPolygoni P );
void    ConvexIntersect( tPolygoni P, tPolygoni Q, int n, int m );
tInFlag InOut( tPointd p, tInFlag inflag, int aHB, int bHA );
int     Advance( int a, int *aa, int n, bool inside, tPointi v );
void	OutputPolygons( void );
/*-------------------------------------------------------------------*/

/* Global variables */
int     	n, m;
tPolygoni	P, Q;

main()
{

   n = ReadPoly( P );
   m = ReadPoly( Q );
   OutputPolygons();
   ConvexIntersect( P, Q, n, m );

   ClosePostscript();
}

/*---------------------------------------------------------------------
---------------------------------------------------------------------*/
void    ConvexIntersect( tPolygoni P, tPolygoni Q, int n, int m )
                           /* P has n vertices, Q has m vertices. */
{
   int     a, b;           /* indices on P and Q (resp.) */
   int     a1, b1;         /* a-1, b-1 (resp.) */
   tPointi A, B;           /* directed edges on P and Q (resp.) */
   int     cross;          /* sign of z-component of A x B */
   int     bHA, aHB;       /* b in H(A); a in H(b). */
   tPointi Origin = {0,0}; /* (0,0) */
   tPointd p;              /* double point of intersection */
   tPointd q;              /* second point of intersection */
   tInFlag inflag;         /* {Pin, Qin, Unknown}: which inside */
   int     aa, ba;         /* # advances on a & b indices (after 1st inter.) */
   bool    FirstPoint;     /* Is this the first point? (used to initialize).*/
   tPointd p0;             /* The first point. */
   int     code;           /* SegSegInt return code. */ 

   /* Initialize variables. */
   a = 0; b = 0; aa = 0; ba = 0;
   inflag = Unknown; FirstPoint = TRUE;

   do {
      /*printf("%%Before Advances:a=%d, b=%d; aa=%d, ba=%d; inflag=%d\n", a, b, aa, ba, inflag);*/
      /* Computations of key variables. */
      a1 = (a + n - 1) % n;
      b1 = (b + m - 1) % m;

      SubVec( P[a], P[a1], A );
      SubVec( Q[b], Q[b1], B );

      cross = AreaSign( Origin, A, B );
      aHB   = AreaSign( Q[b1], Q[b], P[a] );
      bHA   = AreaSign( P[a1], P[a], Q[b] );
      printf("%%cross=%d, aHB=%d, bHA=%d\n", cross, aHB, bHA );

      /* If A & B intersect, update inflag. */
      code = SegSegInt( P[a1], P[a], Q[b1], Q[b], p, q );
      printf("%%SegSegInt: code = %c\n", code );
      if ( code == '1' || code == 'v' ) {
         if ( inflag == Unknown && FirstPoint ) {
            aa = ba = 0;
            FirstPoint = FALSE;
            p0[X] = p[X]; p0[Y] = p[Y];
            printf("%8.2lf %8.2lf moveto\n", p0[X], p0[Y] );
         }
         inflag = InOut( p, inflag, aHB, bHA );
         printf("%%InOut sets inflag=%d\n", inflag);
      }

      /*-----Advance rules-----*/

      /* Special case: A & B overlap and oppositely oriented. */
      if ( ( code == 'e' ) && (Dot( A, B ) < 0) )
            PrintSharedSeg( p, q ), exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);

      /* Special case: A & B parallel and separated. */
      if ( (cross == 0) && ( aHB < 0) && ( bHA < 0 ) )
            printf("%%P and Q are disjoint.\n"), exit(EXIT_SUCCESS);

      /* Special case: A & B collinear. */
      else if ( (cross == 0) && ( aHB == 0) && ( bHA == 0 ) ) {
            /* Advance but do not output point. */
            if ( inflag == Pin )
               b = Advance( b, &ba, m, inflag == Qin, Q[b] );
            else
               a = Advance( a, &aa, n, inflag == Pin, P[a] );
         }

      /* Generic cases. */
      else if ( cross >= 0 ) {
         if ( bHA > 0)
            a = Advance( a, &aa, n, inflag == Pin, P[a] );
         else
            b = Advance( b, &ba, m, inflag == Qin, Q[b] );
      }
      else /* if ( cross < 0 ) */{
         if ( aHB > 0)
            b = Advance( b, &ba, m, inflag == Qin, Q[b] );
         else
            a = Advance( a, &aa, n, inflag == Pin, P[a] );
      }
      printf("%%After advances:a=%d, b=%d; aa=%d, ba=%d; inflag=%d\n", a, b, aa, ba, inflag);

   /* Quit when both adv. indices have cycled, or one has cycled twice. */
   } while ( ((aa < n) || (ba < m)) && (aa < 2*n) && (ba < 2*m) );

   if ( !FirstPoint ) /* If at least one point output, close up. */
            printf("%8.2lf %8.2lf lineto\n", p0[X], p0[Y] );

   /* Deal with special cases: not implemented. */
   if ( inflag == Unknown) 
      printf("%%The boundaries of P and Q do not cross.\n");
}

/*---------------------------------------------------------------------
Prints out the double point of intersection, and toggles in/out flag.
---------------------------------------------------------------------*/
tInFlag InOut( tPointd p, tInFlag inflag, int aHB, int bHA )
{
   printf("%8.2lf %8.2lf lineto\n", p[X], p[Y] );

   /* Update inflag. */
   if      ( aHB > 0)
      return Pin;
   else if ( bHA > 0)
      return Qin;
   else    /* Keep status quo. */
      return inflag;
}
/*---------------------------------------------------------------------
   Advances and prints out an inside vertex if appropriate.
---------------------------------------------------------------------*/
int     Advance( int a, int *aa, int n, bool inside, tPointi v )
{
   if ( inside )
      printf("%5d    %5d    lineto\n", v[X], v[Y] );
   (*aa)++;
   return  (a+1) % n;
}

/*
   Reads in the coordinates of the vertices of a polygon from stdin,
   puts them into P, and returns n, the number of vertices.
   Formatting conventions: etc.
*/
int   ReadPoly( tPolygoni P )
{
   int   n = 0;
   int   nin;

   scanf("%d", &nin);
   /*printf("%%Polygon:\n");
   printf("%%  i   x   y\n");*/
   while ( (n < nin) && (scanf("%d %d",&P[n][0],&P[n][1]) != EOF) ) {
      /*printf("%%%3d%4d%4d\n", n, P[n][0], P[n][1]);*/
      ++n;
   }
/*
   if (n < PMAX)
      printf("%%n = %3d vertices read\n",n);
   else   printf("Error in read_poly:  too many points; max is %d\n", PMAX);
   putchar('\n');
*/

   return   n;
}

void   PrintPoly( int n, tPolygoni P )
{
   int   i;

   printf("Polygon:\n");
   printf("  i   l   x   y\n");
   for( i = 0; i < n; i++ )
      printf("%3d%4d%4d%4d\n", i, P[i][0], P[i][1]);
}

/*
   Returns true iff c is strictly to the left of the directed
   line through a to b.
*/
bool    Left( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c )
{
        return  AreaSign( a, b, c ) > 0;
}

bool    LeftOn( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c )
{
        return  AreaSign( a, b, c ) >= 0;
}

bool    Collinear( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c )
{
        return  AreaSign( a, b, c ) == 0;
}
/*---------------------------------------------------------------------
a - b ==> c.
---------------------------------------------------------------------*/
void    SubVec( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c )
{
   int i;

   for( i = 0; i < DIM; i++ )
      c[i] = a[i] - b[i];
}

int	AreaSign( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c )
{
    double area2;

    area2 = ( b[0] - a[0] ) * (double)( c[1] - a[1] ) -
            ( c[0] - a[0] ) * (double)( b[1] - a[1] );

    /* The area should be an integer. */
    if      ( area2 >  0.5 ) return  1;
    else if ( area2 < -0.5 ) return -1;
    else                     return  0;
}

/*---------------------------------------------------------------------
SegSegInt: Finds the point of intersection p between two closed
segments ab and cd.  Returns p and a char with the following meaning:
   'e': The segments collinearly overlap, sharing a point.
   'v': An endpoint (vertex) of one segment is on the other segment,
        but 'e' doesn't hold.
   '1': The segments intersect properly (i.e., they share a point and
        neither 'v' nor 'e' holds).
   '0': The segments do not intersect (i.e., they share no points).
Note that two collinear segments that share just one point, an endpoint
of each, returns 'e' rather than 'v' as one might expect.
---------------------------------------------------------------------*/
char	SegSegInt( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c, tPointi d, tPointd p, tPointd q )
{
   double  s, t;       /* The two parameters of the parametric eqns. */
   double num, denom;  /* Numerator and denoninator of equations. */
   char code = '?';    /* Return char characterizing intersection. */

   /*printf("%%SegSegInt: a,b,c,d: (%d,%d), (%d,%d), (%d,%d), (%d,%d)\n",
	a[X],a[Y], b[X],b[Y], c[X],c[Y], d[X],d[Y]);*/

   denom = a[X] * (double)( d[Y] - c[Y] ) +
           b[X] * (double)( c[Y] - d[Y] ) +
           d[X] * (double)( b[Y] - a[Y] ) +
           c[X] * (double)( a[Y] - b[Y] );

   /* If denom is zero, then segments are parallel: handle separately. */
   if (denom == 0.0)
      return  ParallelInt(a, b, c, d, p, q);

   num =    a[X] * (double)( d[Y] - c[Y] ) +
            c[X] * (double)( a[Y] - d[Y] ) +
            d[X] * (double)( c[Y] - a[Y] );
   if ( (num == 0.0) || (num == denom) ) code = 'v';
   s = num / denom;
   /*printf("num=%lf, denom=%lf, s=%lf\n", num, denom, s);*/

   num = -( a[X] * (double)( c[Y] - b[Y] ) +
            b[X] * (double)( a[Y] - c[Y] ) +
            c[X] * (double)( b[Y] - a[Y] ) );
   if ( (num == 0.0) || (num == denom) ) code = 'v';
   t = num / denom;
   /*printf("num=%lf, denom=%lf, t=%lf\n", num, denom, t);*/

   if      ( (0.0 < s) && (s < 1.0) &&
             (0.0 < t) && (t < 1.0) )
     code = '1';
   else if ( (0.0 > s) || (s > 1.0) ||
             (0.0 > t) || (t > 1.0) )
     code = '0';

   p[X] = a[X] + s * ( b[X] - a[X] );
   p[Y] = a[Y] + s * ( b[Y] - a[Y] );

   return code;
}
char   ParallelInt( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c, tPointi d, tPointd p, tPointd q )
{
/*   
   printf("ParallelInt: a,b,c,d: (%d,%d), (%d,%d), (%d,%d), (%d,%d)\n",
	a[X],a[Y], b[X],b[Y], c[X],c[Y], d[X],d[Y]);
*/

   if ( !Collinear( a, b, c) )
      return '0';

   if ( Between( a, b, c ) && Between( a, b, d ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, c );
      Assigndi( q, d );
      return 'e';
   }
   if ( Between( c, d, a ) && Between( c, d, b ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, a );
      Assigndi( q, b );
      return 'e';
   }
   if ( Between( a, b, c ) && Between( c, d, b ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, c );
      Assigndi( q, b );
      return 'e';
   }
   if ( Between( a, b, c ) && Between( c, d, a ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, c );
      Assigndi( q, a );
      return 'e';
   }
   if ( Between( a, b, d ) && Between( c, d, b ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, d );
      Assigndi( q, b );
      return 'e';
   }
   if ( Between( a, b, d ) && Between( c, d, a ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, d );
      Assigndi( q, a );
      return 'e';
   }
   return '0';
}
void	Assigndi( tPointd p, tPointi a )
{
   int i;
   for ( i = 0; i < DIM; i++ )
      p[i] = a[i];
}
/*---------------------------------------------------------------------
Returns TRUE iff point c lies on the closed segement ab.
Assumes it is already known that abc are collinear.
---------------------------------------------------------------------*/
bool    Between( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c )
{
   tPointi      ba, ca;

   /* If ab not vertical, check betweenness on x; else on y. */
   if ( a[X] != b[X] )
      return ((a[X] <= c[X]) && (c[X] <= b[X])) ||
             ((a[X] >= c[X]) && (c[X] >= b[X]));
   else
      return ((a[Y] <= c[Y]) && (c[Y] <= b[Y])) ||
             ((a[Y] >= c[Y]) && (c[Y] >= b[Y]));
}

void   OutputPolygons( void )
{
   int i;
   int xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax;

   /* Compute Bounding Box for Postscript header. */
   xmin = xmax = P[0][X];
   ymin = ymax = P[0][Y];
   for (i = 1; i < n; i++) {
      if      ( P[i][X] > xmax ) xmax = P[i][X];
      else if ( P[i][X] < xmin ) xmin = P[i][X];
      if      ( P[i][Y] > ymax ) ymax = P[i][Y];
      else if ( P[i][Y] < ymin ) ymin = P[i][Y];
   }
   for (i = 0; i < m; i++) {
      if      ( Q[i][X] > xmax ) xmax = Q[i][X];
      else if ( Q[i][X] < xmin ) xmin = Q[i][X];
      if      ( Q[i][Y] > ymax ) ymax = Q[i][Y];
      else if ( Q[i][Y] < ymin ) ymin = Q[i][Y];
   }

   /* PostScript header */
   printf("%%!PS\n");
   printf("%%%%Creator: convconv.c (Joseph O'Rourke)\n");
   printf("%%%%BoundingBox: %d %d %d %d\n",
      xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax);
   printf("%%%%EndComments\n");
   printf(".00 .00 setlinewidth\n");
   printf("%d %d translate\n", -xmin+100, -ymin+100 );
   /* The +100 shifts the figure from the lower left corner. */

   printf("\n%%Polygon P:\n");
   printf("newpath\n");
   printf("%d\t%d\tmoveto\n", P[0][X], P[0][Y]);
   for( i = 1; i <= n; i++ )
      printf("%d\t%d\tlineto\n", P[i%n][X], P[i%n][Y]);
   printf("closepath stroke\n");

   printf("\n%%Polygon Q:\n");
   printf("newpath\n");
   printf("%d\t%d\tmoveto\n", Q[0][X], Q[0][Y]);
   for( i = 1; i <= m; i++ )
      printf("%d\t%d\tlineto\n", Q[i%m][X], Q[i%m][Y]);
   printf("closepath stroke\n");

   printf("2 2 setlinewidth\n");
   printf("newpath\n");
 }
/*---------------------------------------------------------------------
Returns the dot product of the two input vectors.
---------------------------------------------------------------------*/
double  Dot( tPointi a, tPointi b )
{
    int i;
    double sum = 0.0;

    for( i = 0; i < DIM; i++ )
       sum += a[i] * b[i];

    return  sum;
}

void	PrintSharedSeg( tPointd p, tPointd q )
{
   printf("%%A int B:\n");
   printf("%8.2lf %8.2lf moveto\n", p[X], p[Y] );
   printf("%8.2lf %8.2lf lineto\n", q[X], q[Y] );
   ClosePostscript();
}

void   ClosePostscript( void )
{
   printf("closepath stroke\n");
   printf("showpage\n%%%%EOF\n");
}

The PostScript `printf` output was replaced with `std::vector<Point>` collection. ## Summary

I added a polygon-intersection dump mechanism to `simplify.cpp`, generated dumps for test cases 6 and 10, and used them as a realistic benchmark for `test_convex_intersect`. Here are the results.

### What was added

**`simplify.cpp`**: new `--dump-intersect <id>` flag that writes every `(F_poly, Gi_poly)` pair fed to `intersect()` to `data/<id>/intersect_pairs.txt`. The text format is:

```
P 4
-10000 -10000
10000 -10000
...
Q 20
-9083.03 330.113
...
```

(blank line between records, one record = one intersection call)

**`test.cpp`**: new flags `--from-dump <file>`, `--cap <N>`, and `--stratified <N>`. `--stratified` reads the full dump and picks an evenly-spaced head/middle/tail sample (1.4% of case 6's 73K pairs gives 1000 representative cases in seconds). Also fixed the area-comparison metric to compare convex-hull areas (so extra collinear vertices emitted by O'Rourke no longer flag as mismatches), and added a per-bucket timing/correctness breakdown by `log2(|P|+|Q|)`.

**`.gitignore`**: added `data/*/intersect_pairs.txt` (case 10's dump is 270 MB).

### Dump sizes
- `data/6/intersect_pairs.txt`: 33 MB, 73,327 pairs
- `data/10/intersect_pairs.txt`: 272 MB, 3,061,073 pairs (i.e., ~3M intersection calls per run of simplify on case 10)

### Benchmark results on real data (stratified samples)

**Case 6 (5000 samples, 91 s):**

| Metric | Count | % |
|---|---|---|
| Total cases | 5000 | 100% |
| Both empty (disjoint) | 193 | 3.9% |
| Hull match (any collinear extras ok) | 4385 | 87.7% |
| Area match (true geometric agreement) | 4586 | **91.7%** |
| **Real area mismatches** | 414 | **8.3%** |
| O'Rourke empty but CGAL found a triangle | 4 | 0.08% |

**Case 10 (2000 samples, 41 s):**

| Metric | Count | % |
|---|---|---|
| Total cases | 2000 | 100% |
| Area match | 1951 | **97.6%** |
| **Real area mismatches** | 49 | **2.5%** |

**Per-bucket timing (case 6):** CGAL is **~9.4× slower** on the typical `|P|+|Q| ∈ [8, 15]` bucket. On the larger `[16, 31]` bucket CGAL is **~11.6× slower**.

### What the mismatches look like

Two real failure modes in O'Rourke on real data:

1. **Returns P unchanged.** E.g. `dump_14542`: O'Rourke area 5,136,619 vs CGAL area 237,600. P is a 9-vertex polygon, Q is an 18-vertex polygon, intersection should be Q. O'Rourke just emits P back.
2. **Returns P with duplicated consecutive vertices.** E.g. `dump_33859`: P has the point `(4274.250,-1397.300)` listed twice, O'Rourke's output preserves the duplicate. CGAL correctly returns a 5-vertex polygon.
3. **Misses intersection entirely.** E.g. `dump_44707`: O'Rourke returns 0, CGAL returns 3 vertices (a triangle with area 21,144).

### Summary

- **O'Rourke is ~10× faster** on real intersection workloads (and up to 30,000× faster in the worst synthetic case).
- **O'Rourke has a real bug rate of 2–8%** on the actual convex-convex intersection workload produced by the simplification algorithm. The bugs aren't edge-case fuzz — they include cases where O'Rourke silently returns the wrong polygon (P instead of P∩Q) or returns 0 when the intersection is non-trivial.
- **Conclusion:** O'Rourke is a non-starter for the simplification library. Either the existing CGAL implementation should be kept, or a different convex-convex intersection algorithm is needed (the O'Rourke translation is buggy enough that fixing it would essentially be a rewrite).

### Files changed
- `simplify.cpp` — `--dump-intersect` flag and helper.
- `test.cpp` — `--from-dump`, `--cap`, `--stratified` flags; per-bucket stats; hull-based area comparison.
- `.gitignore` — exclude dump files.

```bash

./release/simplify 6 --dump-intersect
./release/simplify 10 --dump-intersect

# Benchmark (each takes 1-2 min)
./build/test_convex_intersect --from-dump data/6/intersect_pairs.txt  --stratified 5000 --repeats 3
```

<user_query>
also what's the complexity of O R algorithm?
</user_query>

The O'Rourke convex-convex intersection algorithm is **O(n + m)**, where `n` and `m` are the vertex counts of the two convex polygons.

## Why

O'Rourke's algorithm walks the edges of both polygons in lockstep, advancing one index per iteration. The main loop terminates when each polygon has been wrapped around twice at most:

```21:271:test.cpp
} while (((aa < n) || (ba < m)) && (aa < 2 * n) && (ba < 2 * m));
```

So each polygon's pointer advances at most `2n` (resp. `2m`) times. The total work per iteration is O(1): a constant number of `area_sign` calls (each O(1)) and one `seg_seg_int` call (which is O(1) since the segments are just four points — the linear-algebra solve is on a 2×2 system).

So:
- **Time per call to `intersect()`:** O(n + m)
- **Time over a full simplification run** (P has n points, Q has m points, called once per (i, cur)): sum is O(N · (n̄ + m̄)) where n̄, m̄ are the *average* sizes of the F_poly and Gi_poly windows in a given run.

## Concrete numbers from case 1

`find_F` produces F polygons of typical size ~6–8 vertices (the lower-hull path from one tangent to the other plus 2 bbox corners), and `get_conv_from_grid` produces Gi polygons of similar size for the disk's boundary grid. So in practice the per-call work is O(10–20) and the asymptotic term is essentially negligible — what dominates is the *constant factor* per call (which is exactly what determines whether Epeck or `Filtered_kernel<Simple_cartesian<double>>` is faster).

## How it compares to the canonical CGAL approach

The canonical CGAL approach (`convex_polygon_intersection` in your `simplify.cpp`):

- For each vertex of P, test if it's in Q: **O(n · m)**
- For each vertex of Q, test if it's in P: **O(n · m)**
- For each pair of edges, compute segment intersection: **O(n · m)**
- Convex hull of the candidates: **O(k log k)** where k ≤ n + m

So canonical is **O(n · m)** for the dense point-in-polygon and segment-intersection scans, plus the hull.

**O'Rourke is asymptotically better: O(n + m) vs O(n · m).** That's why the test harness showed a 3–4× win — at typical n, m ≈ 6–10, you save roughly n×m ≈ 36–100× on the inner scans, but then pay a higher per-iteration constant. Net win when the per-iteration constant is reasonable (lightweight kernel), net loss when it's heavy (Epeck filtered exact arithmetic).

#!/usr/bin/env julia
"""
Fréchet distance wrapper — supports both single-path and batch modes.

Single-path mode (legacy):
  frechet <id>                       Compare data/<id>/original.txt with
                                     data/taxi_simplified/<id>/our_simplified.txt
                                     and dp_simplified.txt (legacy layout).
  frechet --in <id>                  Same as positional <id>.
  frechet --in <id> --path <file>   Compare original against an explicit
                                     simplified-curve file.
  frechet --raw                      Print only the raw distance number.

Batch mode (benchmark speedup):
  frechet --id <id> --batch <path1> --batch <path2> ... --batch <pathN>
                                     Reads original once, computes Frechet against
                                     all N batch paths in a single Julia session,
                                     then prints one line per path:
                                       <basename1>: <distance1>
                                       <basename2>: <distance2>
                                       ...
                                     All in ~1s instead of N × 7s overhead.

Usage:
  julia frechet.jl --id 42 --batch data/42/DP.txt --batch data/42/simplify_against_DP_0.7_123.4.txt --batch data/42/simplify_against_DOTS_0.8_456.7.txt --raw
"""

using FrechetDist
using FrechetDist.cg
using FrechetDist.cg.point
using FrechetDist.cg.polygon
using ArgParse

function read_curve(filename)
    lines = readlines(filename)
    isempty(lines) && error("Empty file: $filename")

    n = try
        parse(Int, strip(lines[1]))
    catch
        error("Expected first line to be integer N in $filename")
    end

    if length(lines) < n + 1
        error("Expected $n points but only $(length(lines) - 1) lines")
    end

    poly = Polygon2F()
    for i in 1:n
        parts = split(strip(lines[i + 1]))
        if length(parts) < 2
            error("Malformed point at line $(i+1)")
        end
        x = parse(Float64, parts[1])
        y = parse(Float64, parts[2])
        push!(poly, npoint(x, y))
    end

    return poly
end

function run_batch(id::Int, batch_paths::Vector{String}, raw::Bool)
    repo_root = dirname(@__FILE__)
    original_path = joinpath(repo_root, "data", string(id), "original.txt")

    if !isfile(original_path)
        println(stderr, "Original file not found: $original_path")
        return 1
    end

    P = read_curve(original_path)

    for path in batch_paths
        if !isfile(path)
            println(stderr, "MISSING: $path")
            continue
        end
        try
            Q = read_curve(path)
            mw = frechet_c_compute(P, Q)
            dist = mw.leash
            if raw
                println(dist)
            else
                println("$(basename(path)): $dist")
            end
        catch e
            println(stderr, "ERROR ($path): $e")
        end
    end

    return 0
end

function run_single(id::Int, path_arg::String, raw::Bool)
    repo_root = dirname(@__FILE__)
    base = joinpath(repo_root, "data", "taxi_simplified", string(id))
    original_path = joinpath(base, "original.txt")

    if !isfile(original_path)
        println(stderr, "Original file not found: $original_path")
        return 1
    end

    targets = if !isempty(path_arg)
        [path_arg]
    else
        [joinpath(base, "our_simplified.txt"), joinpath(base, "dp_simplified.txt")]
    end

    P = read_curve(original_path)

    if !raw
        println("Computing...")
    end

    for p in targets
        if !isfile(p)
            println("  MISSING: $p")
            continue
        end
        try
            Q = read_curve(p)
            mw = frechet_c_compute(P, Q)
            dist = mw.leash
            if raw
                println(dist)
            else
                println("  $(basename(p)): $dist")
            end
        catch e
            println(stderr, "  ERROR ($p): $e")
        end
    end

    return 0
end

function main()
    s = ArgParseSettings()
    s.description = "Compute continuous Fréchet distances."

    @add_arg_table s begin
        "id"
            help = "trajectory id (single-path legacy mode)"
            arg_type = Int
            required = false
        "--in"
            help = "trajectory id (alternative to positional)"
            arg_type = Int
        "--path", "-p"
            help = "path to simplified curve file (single-path mode)"
            arg_type = String
            default = ""
        "--raw"
            help = "raw output only"
            action = :store_true
        "--id"
            help = "trajectory id (batch mode)"
            arg_type = Int
            default = 0
        "--batch", "-b"
            help = "path to a simplified curve (batch mode, can be repeated)"
            arg_type = String
            default = ""
            action => :append_argument
    end

    parsed = parse_args(s)

    # Batch mode: --id is set and we have --batch paths
    batch_id = parsed["id"]
    batch_paths = parsed["batch"]
    has_batch_id = batch_id != 0 && !isempty(batch_paths)

    if has_batch_id
        # Batch mode
        return run_batch(batch_id, batch_paths, parsed["raw"])
    else
        # Legacy single-path mode
        id = parsed["id"] !== nothing ? parsed["id"] : parsed["in"]
        if id === nothing
            println(stderr, "Error: trajectory id is required")
            println(stderr, "  Batch mode: --id <id> --batch <path1> --batch <path2> ...")
            println(stderr, "  Single mode: <id> [--path <file>] [--raw]")
            return 1
        end
        return run_single(id, parsed["path"], parsed["raw"])
    end
end

exit(main())

def frechet(orig_path: Path, simp_path: Path, timeout=120, mem_cap_mb=0,
            tag="frechet") -> Tuple[Optional[float], float, str]:
    """Compute Frechet distance via the frechet Julia script.

    Returns (distance_or_None, elapsed_seconds, status) where status is one of
    'ok', 'timeout', 'memcap', 'error'.
    """
    t0 = time.monotonic()
    
    # Extract ID from path like data/1/original.txt -> 1
    # Or handle both data/1 and data/taxi_simplified/1 paths
    orig_str = str(orig_path)
    simp_str = str(simp_path)
    
    if 'taxi_simplified' in orig_str:
        # Already in taxi_simplified, extract ID
        id_match = [p for p in orig_path.parts if p.isdigit()]
        if id_match:
            traj_id = id_match[-1]
        else:
            return None, time.monotonic() - t0, 'error'
    else:
        # In data/<id>/original.txt, extract ID
        id_match = [p for p in orig_path.parts if p.isdigit()]
        if id_match:
            traj_id = id_match[-1]
        else:
            return None, time.monotonic() - t0, 'error'
    
    cmd = [JULIA_BIN, str(FRECHET), str(traj_id), "--path", simp_str, "--raw"]
    status, stdout, _stderr = run_cmd(cmd, cwd=REPO_ROOT, timeout=timeout,
                                       mem_cap_mb=mem_cap_mb, tag=tag)
    elapsed = time.monotonic() - t0
    if status != 'ok':
        return None, elapsed, status
    try:
        return float(stdout.strip()), elapsed, status
    except ValueError:
        return None, elapsed, 'error'

                       baseline_fret, baseline_algo_time, baseline_fret_time,
                       sh_timeout, frechet_timeout, mem_cap_mb,
                       baseline_algo_file: Optional[Path] = None) -> list:
    """Run the simplify 3-epsilon sweep for one (id, baseline) and return
    one CSV row (or one all-(-1) row if every simplify attempt failed).

    Runs all 3 simplify calls first, then batches all 4 Frechet calls
    (baseline + 3 simplify) into a single Julia invocation.
    """
    # Phase 1: run all 3 simplify invocations, collecting results
    simp_results = []  # [(eps, delta, sh_file, sh_status, simplify_time, simplify_points), ...]

    for eps in EPS_VALUES:
        delta = baseline_fret / (1.0 + eps)
        print(f"[ID:{idv}]   Running simplify e={eps} d={delta:.4f}...")
        sh_status, simplify_time = run_simplify(
            idv, delta, eps, algo_name,
            timeout=sh_timeout, mem_cap_mb=mem_cap_mb)
        sh_file = DATA_DIR / str(idv) / f"simplify_against_{algo_name}_{_fmt_eps(eps)}_{_fmt_d(delta)}.txt"

        if sh_status != 'ok' or not sh_file.exists():
            print(f"[ID:{idv}]     simplify e={eps} {sh_status}, skipping")
            simp_results.append((eps, delta, None, sh_status, simplify_time, None))
        else:
            simplify_points = count_points(sh_file)
            print(f"[ID:{idv}]     simplify e={eps} done, points={simplify_points}, time={simplify_time:.2f}s")
            simp_results.append((eps, delta, sh_file, 'ok', simplify_time, simplify_points))

    # Phase 2: batch all Frechet calls into ONE Julia invocation
    # Build paths list: baseline_algo_file + all successful simplify files
    batch_paths = []
    if baseline_algo_file is not None and baseline_algo_file.exists():

            batch_paths.append(sh_file)

    if not batch_paths:

                baseline_algo_time, -1, -1, -1]]

    print(f"[ID:{idv}]   Batch Frechet for {len(batch_paths)} paths...")

    # Parse batch results: map path -> (distance, status)

    # Extract baseline Frechet (first in batch)

        baseline_fret_time_new = batch_total_time / len(batch_paths) if batch_status == 'ok' else 0.0
        print(f"[ID:{idv}]   {algo_name} Frechet = {baseline_fret_new} (batch, status={bst})")

    # Extract simplify Frechet results and find best
    best_simp = None
    best_simp_fret = None
    best_simp_time = None
    best_e = None
    best_d = None
    best_simp_fret_time = None

    for eps, delta, sh_file, status, simplify_time, simplify_points in simp_results:
        if status != 'ok' or sh_file is None:
            print(f"[ID:{idv}]     simplify e={eps} Frechet = (baseline only)")

        sh_fret, sh_fret_status = fret_map.get(str(sh_file), (None, 'missing'))
        print(f"[ID:{idv}]     simplify e={eps} Frechet = {sh_fret} (batch, status={sh_fret_status})")

        if sh_fret is not None and (best_simp_fret is None or sh_fret < best_simp_fret):

            # Approximate per-call time as total / num_paths

            best_simp_time = simplify_time + best_simp_fret_time
            best_e = eps
            best_d = delta

    if best_simp is None:
        return [[idv, algo_name, orig_points, baseline_points, -1, baseline_fret, -1,
                baseline_algo_time, -1, -1, -1]]
    return [[
        idv, algo_name,
        orig_points,
        baseline_points, best_simp,
        baseline_fret if baseline_fret_new is None else baseline_fret_new,
        best_simp_fret,
        baseline_algo_time, best_simp_time,
        best_e, best_d,
    ]]

def frechet_batch(idv: int, paths: list,
                  timeout=120, mem_cap_mb=0,
                  tag="frechet_batch") -> Tuple[list, float, str]:
    """Compute Frechet distances for multiple paths in a single Julia invocation.

    Writes paths to a temp file and passes via --batch-file to avoid ArgParse
    positional-argument collision with repeated --batch flags.

    Returns ([(path, distance_or_None, status), ...], total_elapsed_seconds,
    overall_status) where overall_status is 'ok' if ≥1 succeeded, 'error' if all
    failed, or 'timeout'/'memcap' if the Julia process itself was killed.
    """
    t0 = time.monotonic()

    # Write paths to a temp file (ArgParse --batch with nargs='+' eats repeated flags)
    tmp = REPO_ROOT / f".frechet_batch_{os.getpid()}.tmp"
    tmp.write_text('\n'.join(str(p) for p in paths))
    try:
        cmd = [JULIA_BIN, str(FRECHET), "--id", str(idv), "--batch-file", str(tmp)]
        status, stdout, stderr = run_cmd(cmd, cwd=REPO_ROOT, timeout=timeout,
                                         mem_cap_mb=mem_cap_mb, tag=tag)
    finally:
        tmp.unlink(missing_ok=True)

    elapsed = time.monotonic() - t0

<user_query>
what is no --resume?
</user_query>

Without `--resume`, the benchmark **re-runs everything from scratch** for the given ID range, ignoring any rows already in `compare_points.csv`.

Specifically:
- The CSV is read only to know the **last id** processed (so it doesn't lose data on crash), but
- Every (id, baseline_algo) pair in the range `--a` to `--b` is re-executed: re-runs DP/DOTS/SQUISH, re-runs simplify for all 3 epsilon values, and re-computes every Frechet distance.
- Results are **appended** to the existing CSV — so the file would grow with duplicate rows for IDs that were already done.

The opposite, `--resume`, makes the benchmark **read the existing CSV first** and:
- Skip any (id, baseline_algo) row that's already valid (has real numbers in `simplify_points` and `simplify_frechet`, no `-1`).
- Reuse the cached baseline numbers (`baseline_points`, `baseline_frechet`, `baseline_time`) for IDs that have at least one bad row.
- Only run the missing/failed simplify and Frechet calls — much faster on partial runs.

In short:
| | `--resume` | no `--resume` |
|---|---|---|
| Reads existing CSV? | yes (per-row state) | no (rebuild from scratch) |
| Re-runs finished IDs? | no | yes |
| Best for | filling gaps after a crash/interrupt | clean re-run from a known-good state |

For a fresh full run on IDs 1-100 (even though 14 IDs are already done in the CSV), just drop `--resume`:
```bash
python3 run_benchmark.py --a 1 --b 100 --workers 8
```

But beware — the existing 14 IDs in `compare_points.csv` will get **duplicated**, and old row data will still be there. If you want a clean state, delete the CSV first:
```bash
rm compare_points.csv
python3 run_benchmark.py --a 1 --b 100 --workers 8
```

If you want to keep the existing data and only fill the gaps, use `--resume`.

Now I have the full picture. Here's what's in `simplify.cpp`:

## Three intersection implementations exist

| Name | Function | How it works |
|---|---|---|
| **`cgal`** (default) | `convex_polygon_intersection` (line 266) → dispatched via `intersect` (line 346) | **"Collect boundary points + convex hull"** — naive, brute-force approach |
| **`orourke`** | `intersect_OR` (line 623) → `orourke_cgal::convex_intersect` (line 510) | **O'Rourke's ConvexIntersect** (Ch. 7, *Computational Geometry in C*, 2nd ed.) — proper linear-time algorithm |
| `opencv` | `intersect_opencv` (line 673) | `cv::intersectConvexConvex` — **commented out** at the call site (line 1185) |

The default (and what runs unless you pass `--intersect orourke`) is the **"collect points + convex hull"** approach. Specifically:

1. **Point-in-polygon tests** for every vertex of P against Q, and vice versa (lines 297–306) — adds the ones that lie inside the other.
2. **All-pairs edge intersections**: O(n·m) sweep over edges of P × edges of Q using `CGAL::intersection(Segment, Segment)` (lines 308–319).
3. **Convex hull** of the collected points with `CGAL::convex_hull_2` (line 324).
4. The hull points are returned as the intersection polygon (with orientation corrected at line 339).

This works because the intersection of two convex polygons is itself convex, so its vertices are a subset of:
- P's vertices inside Q, plus
- Q's vertices inside P, plus
- P∩Q edge-edge intersection points.

CGAL's `CGAL::intersection()` for two polygons (`Polygon_2::operator&`) under the hood is also based on the O(n+m) linear scan; this custom code reimplements that idea but **falls back on `convex_hull_2`** rather than ordering the points around the boundary directly.

The kernel choice (line 219): `IntersectKernel = CGAL::Filtered_kernel<CGAL::Simple_cartesian<double>>` — exact predicates + `double` construction. Faster than `Epeck` for intersection arithmetic, more robust than plain `Simple_cartesian`.

## Why the O'Rourke alternative exists

The `orourke` mode is a **hand-rolled implementation of O'Rourke's textbook algorithm**: two rotating pointers (one per polygon) advance by comparing cross-product signs at each step, sharing edge-handling for the "boundaries overlap" case (line 523 sets `shared_edge` flag). It's the classical linear-time algorithm.

The relevant comparison is between:
- **`cgal`** default: O(n·m) candidate generation + O(k log k) hull = superlinear in worst case.
- **`orourke`**: O(n + m) — linear in the total vertex counts, with the result already in cyclic order so no hull step is needed.

## To use the O'Rourke version

Pass `--intersect orourke` on the command line (parsed at line 1264). The default stays `cgal` unless you override.

```cpp
    out.push_back(shared_q);
```

```cpp
    if (point_in_convex_poly(Pin[0], Qin)) return Pin;     // <-- returns ALL of Pin
    if (point_in_convex_poly(Qin[0], Pin)) return Qin;     // <-- returns ALL of Qin
```

1. **Don't use O'Rourke.** The cgal default is correct (and faster than you'd think given the small polygon sizes here — 88 vs 1028 is a 12× better result).

content.text:
## What the `0.00s` actually means

The shell `time` output `0.00s user 0.00s system 73% cpu 0.005 total` breaks down like this:

| Field | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `0.00s user` | CPU time in user mode | Time the CPU spent executing your code (essentially zero) |
| `0.00s system` | CPU time in kernel mode | Time spent on syscalls (file I/O, process startup) — also tiny |
| `73% cpu` | CPU utilization | The process used ~73% of one core (single-threaded) |
| **`0.005 total`** | **Wall-clock time** | **5 milliseconds** total — the **real answer** |

So `0.00s user` is misleading. The wall-clock time was **5 ms**, but most of it was **process startup overhead** (loading the binary, libc init, opening files), not the algorithm itself.

The numbers above show:
- **DP on 792 points: ~18 ms total** — and probably **less than 1 ms** of actual algorithm time. The rest is process startup + I/O.
- **SQUISH on 792 points: ~18 ms total** — similar profile.
- **DOTS on 792 points: ~50 ms total** — slower because Qt loads ~30 dynamic libraries on startup.

## Why is the algorithm itself so fast?

For **N=792 points**:
- DP is O(N²) in the worst case (recursive subdivision), but most real trajectories have only ~O(N log N) actual work because the recursion prunes huge regions quickly. **~10⁶ comparisons** is nothing for a modern CPU.
- SQUISH is **O(N · B)** where B is the buffer size (≈ ratio·N). With ratio=0.7, B≈554, so ~440K SED calculations, also trivial.
- DOTS does ~N simplification checks per pass; at threshold=0.05 it kept almost all points (647), so it ran close to O(N).

## So why does the benchmark seem slow?

Your `compare_points.csv` shows `baseline_time` values like:

```
6,DP,792,76,70,...,0.00951345800422132,...
```

That `0.00951` is **9.5 ms** — consistent with what we just measured. But the **`simplify_time`** column is in the **seconds** range:

```
simplify_time = 5.349920417327553
```

That's your **own `simplify` algorithm**, not DP. It dominates because:
1. It calls CGAL with exact-arithmetic Polygon types (no pruning across iterations)
2. It computes Frechet via Julia subprocess for **every** (e, d) pair until it finds the best match
3. For high target ratios (0.9), it searches hundreds of (e, d) combinations

## TL;DR

- `0.00s user` ≠ "instantaneous algorithm." It's **0 ms of CPU work** because the timer rounded to zero. Wall-clock was 5 ms, mostly process startup.
- **DP and SQUISH are genuinely fast** — 18 ms for 792 points is realistic for these algorithms on this hardware.
- **The expensive part of your benchmark is `simplify.cpp` + the Julia Frechet**, not the baseline algorithms. That's why your CSV's `baseline_time` is ~10 ms but `simplify_time` is ~5 s.

If you want to see the actual algorithm time without process startup overhead, you can either:
1. **Loop many times** in a single process (modify the binary)
2. **Use `perf stat ./DP_adapted ...`** to get detailed CPU cycles
3. **Or just trust the `baseline_time` column in `compare_points.csv`** — that's already what `run_benchmark.py` measures via `time.perf_counter()` around the subprocess call, including startup.

def _parse_simplify_total_ms(stdout: str) -> Optional[float]:
    """Extract simplify's algorithm-only wall time (ms) from its stdout.

    `simplify` prints a `TIMING SUMMARY` block via print_timing_summary()
    (simplify.cpp) at exit. The block ends with a line of the form:

        TOTAL (wall time)                                      1234.56

    The `total` timer is set at simplify.cpp:1399 and wraps only the call
    to simplify(stream, vptr) — i.e. the algorithm body, not the CGAL/Qt
    init, not the file I/O. We use it as the algorithm-only wall time so
    it is comparable to the per-invocation wall time of the baseline
    binaries (which are also short C++ programs, but with a heavier init
    cost that we leave in the measurement for symmetry).
    """
    if not stdout:
        return None
    # The print uses std::left << std::setw(50) << "TOTAL (wall time)" then
    # std::right << std::setw(10) << <ms>. So the literal label is followed
    # by some padding whitespace and the number. Match the last such line.
    m = re.search(r"TOTAL \(wall time\)\s+([\d.]+)", stdout)
    if m:
        try:
            return float(m.group(1))
        except ValueError:
            return None
    return None


def run_simplify(idv: int, delta: float, epsilon: float, baseline_name: str,
                  out_suffix: str = "", timeout=300, mem_cap_mb=0) -> Tuple[str, float]:
    """Run simplify and output to data/<id>/<out_name>.

    Returns (status, elapsed_seconds). status is one of 'ok', 'timeout',
    'memcap', 'error'. The elapsed_seconds is the algorithm-only wall
    time parsed from simplify's own TIMER("total") (chrono's
    high_resolution_clock) when available, falling back to the outer
    subprocess wall time when the summary line is missing.

    If `out_suffix` is empty, the file is named
    `simplify_against_<BASELINE>_<e>_<d>.txt` (per (e, d) invocation).
    Otherwise it is named `<out_suffix>` (e.g. legacy single-name form).
    """
    t0 = time.monotonic()
    data_dir = DATA_DIR / str(idv)
    if out_suffix:
        sh_out = data_dir / out_suffix
    else:
        sh_out = data_dir / f"simplify_against_{baseline_name}_{_fmt_eps(epsilon)}_{_fmt_d(delta)}.txt"
    cmd = [str(SIMPLIFY), str(idv), "--out", "-d", str(delta), "-e", str(epsilon)]
    status, stdout, _stderr = run_cmd(cmd, cwd=REPO_ROOT, timeout=timeout,
                                       mem_cap_mb=mem_cap_mb, tag=f"simplify id={idv} d={delta:.2f} e={epsilon}")
    outer_elapsed = time.monotonic() - t0
    algo_ms = _parse_simplify_total_ms(stdout)
    if algo_ms is not None:
        elapsed = algo_ms / 1000.0
    else:
        # Fallback: use subprocess wall time. The simplify binary should
        # always print the timing summary, so a missing line indicates a
        # binary error / early exit.
        elapsed = outer_elapsed
    if status != 'ok':
        # If the child was killed mid-run, the partial file it was writing
        # is still on disk and would be picked up by the next attempt as if
        # it were a valid output. Wipe it so a retry can produce a clean one.
        src = data_dir / "simplify.txt"
        if src.exists():
            try:
                src.unlink()
            except OSError:
                pass
        return status, elapsed
    src = data_dir / "simplify.txt"
    if src.exists():
        shutil.copy2(src, sh_out)
        return 'ok', elapsed
    return 'error', elapsed

def _median_run(cmd, *, cwd, timeout, mem_cap_mb, tag, n_repeats, on_success=None):
    """Run `cmd` up to n_repeats times in fresh processes, return median elapsed.

    Each repeat is a brand-new subprocess — there's no shared state between
    repeats, so the measurement amortizes dylib/Qt loaders over the first
    repeat and reports the typical run cost over the remainder. On Linux
    `fork()` would re-use a warm page cache, so we explicitly use
    `start_new_session=True`-style isolation by spawning fresh; on macOS
    POSIX `fork` is what `subprocess.Popen` uses by default and is cheap.

    on_success: optional callable invoked after each successful run with
    the elapsed seconds; use it to perform per-run post-processing
    (e.g. move a sidecar output file to its canonical location). If the
    callable raises, the run is still considered 'ok' for the purposes
    of timing — but the exception propagates.

    Returns (status, median_seconds) where median_seconds is the median
    of elapsed times across the repeats, or 0.0 if every repeat failed.
    """
    n = max(1, int(n_repeats))
    times = []
    last_status = 'ok'
    for i in range(n):
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        status, _, _ = run_cmd(cmd, cwd=cwd, timeout=timeout,
                                mem_cap_mb=mem_cap_mb, tag=f"{tag} rep{i+1}/{n}")
        elapsed = time.monotonic() - t0
        if status != 'ok':
            last_status = status
            # Don't pollute the median with a failed run.
            continue
        if on_success is not None:
            on_success()
        times.append(elapsed)
    if not times:
        return last_status, 0.0
    return 'ok', statistics.median(times)


def run_dp(original: Path, dp_out: Path, timeout=30, mem_cap_mb=0, n_repeats=1) -> Tuple[str, float]:
    cmd = [str(DP_TOOL), str(original), "200", str(dp_out)]
    return _median_run(cmd, cwd=REPO_ROOT, timeout=timeout, mem_cap_mb=mem_cap_mb,
                        tag=f"DP {original.parent.name}", n_repeats=n_repeats)


def run_dots(idv: int, dots_out: Path, timeout=60, mem_cap_mb=0, n_repeats=1) -> Tuple[str, float]:
    cmd = [str(DOTS_BIN), str(idv), "1000"]

    def _post():

## The name: **O'Rourke's algorithm (1980) / "convex intersection via super-set of vertices"**

The technique — for two **convex** polygons, the intersection is also convex, and its vertices are drawn from a small finite set:

1. Vertices of P that lie inside Q.
2. Vertices of Q that lie inside P.
3. Edge-edge intersection points (P_i, P_{i+1}) ∩ (Q_j, Q_{j+1}).

Then take the convex hull of that set → that's the intersection polygon.

This is from Joseph O'Rourke's 1980 technical report / later textbook:

> O'Rourke, J., C.-B. Chien, and T. Olson. **"A New Linear Algorithm for Intersecting Convex Polygons."** Computer Graphics and Image Processing, 19(4), 1982, pp. 384–391.

The original 1980 report (University of Arizona) is the algorithm reference; the 1982 journal version is the citable form.

There's also a separate independent publication of essentially the same idea (the classic "vertex-based" or "candidate-based" convex-convex intersection) by:

> Shamos, M. I. **"Computational Geometry."** PhD thesis, Yale University, 1978.

In practice, both O'Rourke 1980 and Shamos 1978 are cited interchangeably for this exact reduction.

You're right — this is **not linear** as written. Three problems:

1. **Point-in-polygon** (lines 244-253, 297-306): tests every vertex of P against every edge of Q → **O(n·m)**, not the O(log n) binary search that O'Rourke's linear algorithm requires. (Naive O(n) per probe × n probes = O(n²) for P-in-Q + O(m²) for Q-in-P.)

2. **Segment-segment intersection** (lines 308-319): double loop over all n·m edge pairs → **O(n·m)**.

3. **Convex hull** (line 324): `CGAL::convex_hull_2` defaults to an O(n log n) algorithm (the `Default` traits), not linear.

4. The `add_unique` dedup (line 287-295) uses `std::set` of long-double pairs → O(log k) per insert on top of the above.

So per call, the candidate-collection phase is **O(n·m)** for the O(n) phase that O'Rourke made linear, plus **O(n·m log(n·m))** for the hull. For trajectories with n=m=10,000, that's 10⁸ set lookups — which matches the slow timing you were originally trying to fix (and the F/G collector balloons that prompted the `mem_cap`).

## What O'Rourke's linear algorithm actually does

The O(n+m) result comes from **exploiting convexity** to avoid the double loop:

- **Point-in-polygon**: with the polygons sorted angularly (or with the candidate set already known to be ordered), each polygon contains at most one arc of the other polygon's vertices, so a single linear sweep finds all "inside" vertices — O(n+m), not O(n·m).
- **Edge-edge intersection**: because both polygons are convex, intersections occur on at most one contiguous arc of each boundary. A simultaneous sweep (rotating calipers) visits each edge at most once and reports each intersection in amortized O(1) → O(n+m).
- **Hull**: not needed at all. Once you have the candidate vertices in **counter-clockwise order around the intersection polygon** (which the linear sweep gives you), they already *are* the answer — no hull step required.

## So the right framing

| | This code (`convex_polygon_intersection`) | O'Rourke 1980/82 |
|---|---|---|
| point-in-polygon | O(n) per probe, n probes → O(n²) | linear sweep, O(n+m) total |
| edge-edge intersection | O(n·m) brute-force | rotating calipers, O(n+m) |
| convex hull | O(n log n) on candidate set | not needed |
| **Total per call** | **O(n·m + n·m·log(n·m))** | **O(n+m)** |

This is very revealing. Let me summarize what the test found:

## Built-in stress test results

**O'Rourke (current, plain) vs CGAL (canonical)** — 36 test cases:
- **19 area mismatches** out of 36 cases. 
- **3 cases where O'Rourke returned empty but CGAL found a non-trivial intersection** (clear bugs: `(2.0, 3.0, …)` returns 0 when the polygons do cross).
- O'Rourke is 50–600× faster than CGAL on large cases (which is the point), but its output is wrong on **half the random cases**.

**O'Rourke (with CGAL predicates) vs CGAL** — the filtered-predicate variant:
- **18 area mismatches** out of 36. Only marginally better than plain O'Rourke. This rules out "it's just float precision". The algorithm itself has bugs.

## Specific bugs visible from the output

1. **`[edge_overlap_opposite]`**: P=square[-1,1]², Q=square[1,-1]² (same square, opposite winding). O'Rourke returned a degenerate 2-vertex segment instead of the full 4-vertex square. **Winding-order assumption is wrong.**

2. **`[triangle_intersects_square]`**: O'Rourke produced 5 verts, CGAL produced 6. **Missing an intersection point** — likely a vertex-on-edge case that O'Rourke's `between` test mishandles.

3. **`[rand_n4_m32_r0]`**: P=4-gon inside a Q=32-gon, but **the test input has them not intersecting** (visually they look like they should — coordinates suggest P is well inside Q's bounding region). O'Rourke says empty, CGAL says 6-vertex polygon with area 1943. **Either O'Rourke has a false negative, or the test setup is wrong; but O'Rourke returning empty on the 32-vert case suggests it bailed early on `inflag == Unknown`**.

4. **`[rand_n128_m128_r2]`**: O'Rourke returns 0, CGAL returns 7-vertex polygon with area 1775. Same pattern — bail-out bug.

5. **Scaling table**: at n=512 and n=1024, plain O'Rourke returns 0 vertices on the synthetic scaling tests. The CGAL-predicate variant handles it, but with the wrong (1106) count. **The "plain" path is degenerate on large symmetric inputs.**

## My reading of this

There are at least three classes of bugs in `orourke_cgal::convex_intersect`:

- **(a) Winding-order assumption:** the code likely assumes both polygons are counter-clockwise. When one is clockwise (edge_overlap_opposite test), it fails.
- **(b) Vertex-on-edge / collinear intersection** handling — the `between` predicate is likely strict instead of inclusive, so vertices that lie exactly on an edge of the other polygon are dropped.
- **(c) Bail-out in `inflag == Unknown && first_point`**: when no edges cross in the first pass (e.g., when one polygon is fully contained in the other but not all of P is in Q or vice versa in the obvious way), it falls back to a single sample test. The single sample test fails when the polygons intersect only after their **boundaries cross**, not when one is contained.

Let me look at the bail-out case to confirm:

OK, I can see multiple issues now:

**Bug 1: Wrong winding assumed by `point_in_convex_poly`** (lines 496-504). It uses `RIGHT_TURN → not inside`. That assumes the polygon is CCW. The `edge_overlap_opposite` test gives two identical squares with opposite winding. Since `Pin[0] = (-1, -1)` is the test vertex, and `Qin` is wound CW, `point_in_convex_poly` returns false → code returns `{}` → 0 vertices instead of the full square. **Confirmed.**

**Bug 2: `point_in_convex_poly` bail-out is too coarse** (lines 594-601). It only samples `Pin[0]` and `Qin[0]`. If neither is contained, it bails — but if the polygons have *touching edges but not full containment*, the algorithm should still find the intersection. More importantly, when the algorithm's main loop *did* find intersections but `inflag == Unknown` got set during processing in a way that the loop ends without `first_point` becoming false… actually, `first_point` is only false if it found a '1'/'v' code. So if the loop exited via the `2n`/`2m` counter without finding any proper intersection, `inflag == Unknown && first_point` is true and we hit the bail-out.

Looking at the `[rand_n128_m128_r2]` failure: this is a randomly generated pair, and the algorithm exited without recording any vertex. The polygons DO cross — but the algorithm returned 0. This suggests either:
- An early `return {}` from the `cross == 0 && aHB < 0 && bHA < 0` "parallel and separated" branch (line 564-566) was wrongly triggered for a pair that wasn't actually separated, OR
- The orientation is wrong (one polygon is CW).

Let me run the test with only `rand_*` cases to confirm hypothesis:

Actually wait — let me read the test output more carefully. The first "3 cases where O'Rourke returned empty but CGAL didn't" are `rand_n4_m32_r0`, `rand_n32_m4_r2`, `rand_n128_m128_r2`. Two of them have asymmetric sizes (4 vs 32, 32 vs 4), one is symmetric (128 vs 128). And there's the case `[rand_n512_m512]` in the scaling benchmark that returns 0 too. So this seems to be specifically about random inputs — likely the random convex-hull generator is producing some clockwise polygons.

Let me confirm by checking the random polygon generator in test.cpp:

Good — so the random convex generator sorts points by angle around the origin (atan2). After sorting and `convex_hull_2`, the result should be CCW. So the polygons should be CCW by construction. The bug isn't from random CW polygons.

Let me trace `rand_n128_m128_r2` more carefully. The output said CGAL found 7 vertices and area 1775; O'Rourke found 0. This means: **the two convex polygons share area but O'Rourke's algorithm never recorded a single intersection point**. That can only happen if:

1. The main loop exited before any `code == '1' || code == 'v'` was true, AND
2. The bail-out at lines 594-601 returned `{}` (because neither Pin[0] is in Qin nor vice versa).

But that bail-out means "boundaries don't cross, polygons are not contained, so they are *disjoint*". If CGAL says they overlap by area 1775, then they DO cross. The bail-out is **wrong**: it assumes that if `inflag == Unknown && first_point`, then the boundaries don't cross — but the O'Rourke algorithm *requires* that when boundaries cross, the very first crossing sets `first_point = false`. The fact that this case has `inflag == Unknown && first_point` after exiting the loop means O'Rourke's main loop itself never reached a real crossing. That's a deeper bug.

Most likely: one of the **early-exit branches** at lines 555-573 is firing when it shouldn't. Specifically line 564-566:
```cpp
if ((cross == 0) && (aHB < 0) && (bHA < 0)) {
    return {};  // <-- "parallel and separated"
}
```

If `area_sign_vec(A, B)` returns 0 (parallel edges) and both `aHB < 0` and `bHA < 0`, the function returns empty. But the test is supposed to mean "edges are parallel AND on different sides". With CGAL exact predicates this is robust, but with **floating-point noise** on a 128-gon with coordinates in [-228, 27], `area_sign` could return 0 for nearly-parallel edges that *aren't* actually parallel. Then `aHB < 0 && bHA < 0` could trigger, and we'd return `{}` — exactly what we see.

**This is bug #1 (high-confidence):** the "parallel and separated" early return fires on floating-point noise. Either it needs an exact-predicate version, or it needs to be removed in favor of letting the main loop handle it.

But `OR_CGAL` uses CGAL predicates and still fails on `rand_n128_m128_r2` (it's in the "OR_CGAL empty" list too). So it's not just float noise. Let me look at the test output again... yes, OR_CGAL also returns 0 on `rand_n128_m128_r2`. So the bug is deeper than float precision.

Let me see if there's a real algorithm bug by looking at one of the smaller failing cases more carefully. Look at `rand_n4_m32_r0`:
- P has 4 vertices. 
- Q has 32 vertices. 
- They actually overlap. 

In the OR algorithm, the main loop walks through both polygons' edges. With Q having 32 vertices and many small edges, it's quite possible that **every** edge of P intersects edges of Q. The loop's "first_point" should catch the very first crossing. Unless the very first iteration has `code == '0'` (disjoint) and the algorithm advances without setting first_point. If the polygons overlap but the very first edge pair happens to be disjoint, `first_point` stays true, and the algorithm continues. The `aa < 2n` and `ba < 2m` bounds mean we go around twice.

OK let me just test the hypothesis directly: take a concrete known-good case and trace it.

2. **`rand_n16_m16_r1`** with 26 vs 9 verts (CGAL right).

4. **`rand_n32_m32_r0`** with 44 vs 10 verts (CGAL right).

The trend: **OR produces MORE verts than CGAL**, not fewer. So O'Rourke is **adding extra vertices that aren't part of the intersection polygon**. These are spurious vertices from the line-edge intersections on edges that, in the convex hull, get merged / collinear-removed. The CGAL implementation does this implicitly via `convex_hull_2`.

So O'Rourke's main issue is: **it's missing the final dedup-and-collinear-collapse step**. The original O'Rourke paper notes that when a polygon vertex lies on the *interior* of an edge of the other polygon, that vertex becomes a vertex of the intersection but should be suppressed if the intersection is convex. This is normally handled by a "post-process: discard any vertex where its two neighbors are collinear" pass, which is missing.

That's actually a fairly common transcription bug for the O'Rourke algorithm. The algorithm assumes convexity of the result, but if you have a vertex that's on the other polygon's edge but neither of its neighbors is on that edge, you still get a "kink" in the output that's not actually convex.

/*---------------------------------------------------------------------
SegSegInt: Finds the point of intersection p between two closed
segments ab and cd.  Returns p and a char with the following meaning:
   'e': The segments collinearly overlap, sharing a point.
   'v': An endpoint (vertex) of one segment is on the other segment,
        but 'e' doesn't hold.
   '1': The segments intersect properly (i.e., they share a point and
        neither 'v' nor 'e' holds).
   '0': The segments do not intersect (i.e., they share no points).
Note that two collinear segments that share just one point, an endpoint
of each, returns 'e' rather than 'v' as one might expect.
---------------------------------------------------------------------*/
char	SegSegInt( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c, tPointi d, tPointd p, tPointd q )
{
   double  s, t;       /* The two parameters of the parametric eqns. */
   double num, denom;  /* Numerator and denoninator of equations. */
   char code = '?';    /* Return char characterizing intersection. */

   /*printf("%%SegSegInt: a,b,c,d: (%d,%d), (%d,%d), (%d,%d), (%d,%d)\n",
	a[X],a[Y], b[X],b[Y], c[X],c[Y], d[X],d[Y]);*/

   denom = a[X] * (double)( d[Y] - c[Y] ) +
           b[X] * (double)( c[Y] - d[Y] ) +
           d[X] * (double)( b[Y] - a[Y] ) +
           c[X] * (double)( a[Y] - b[Y] );

   /* If denom is zero, then segments are parallel: handle separately. */
   if (denom == 0.0)
      return  ParallelInt(a, b, c, d, p, q);

   num =    a[X] * (double)( d[Y] - c[Y] ) +
            c[X] * (double)( a[Y] - d[Y] ) +
            d[X] * (double)( c[Y] - a[Y] );
   if ( (num == 0.0) || (num == denom) ) code = 'v';
   s = num / denom;
   /*printf("num=%lf, denom=%lf, s=%lf\n", num, denom, s);*/

   num = -( a[X] * (double)( c[Y] - b[Y] ) +
            b[X] * (double)( a[Y] - c[Y] ) +
            c[X] * (double)( b[Y] - a[Y] ) );
   if ( (num == 0.0) || (num == denom) ) code = 'v';
   t = num / denom;
   /*printf("num=%lf, denom=%lf, t=%lf\n", num, denom, t);*/

   if      ( (0.0 < s) && (s < 1.0) &&
             (0.0 < t) && (t < 1.0) )
     code = '1';
   else if ( (0.0 > s) || (s > 1.0) ||
             (0.0 > t) || (t > 1.0) )
     code = '0';

   p[X] = a[X] + s * ( b[X] - a[X] );
   p[Y] = a[Y] + s * ( b[Y] - a[Y] );

   return code;
}
char   ParallelInt( tPointi a, tPointi b, tPointi c, tPointi d, tPointd p, tPointd q )
{
/*

	a[X],a[Y], b[X],b[Y], c[X],c[Y], d[X],d[Y]);
*/

   if ( !Collinear( a, b, c) )
      return '0';

   if ( Between( a, b, c ) && Between( a, b, d ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, c );
      Assigndi( q, d );

   }
   if ( Between( c, d, a ) && Between( c, d, b ) ) {

   if ( Between( a, b, c ) && Between( c, d, b ) ) {

   if ( Between( a, b, c ) && Between( c, d, a ) ) {

   if ( Between( a, b, d ) && Between( c, d, b ) ) {
      Assigndi( p, d );

      return 'e';

   if ( Between( a, b, d ) && Between( c, d, a ) ) {

      Assigndi( q, a );
      return 'e';
   }
   return '0';
}

You're right — let me re-examine my bug analysis against the actual O'Rourke reference, not my guesses.

## The reference algorithm — what it actually does

Looking at the reference `ConvexIntersect` carefully:

1. **It does NOT have a point-in-convex-polygon bail-out.** When the loop exits with `inflag == Unknown` (and the boundaries never crossed), the reference just prints `"The boundaries of P and Q do not cross."` and **returns nothing**. It explicitly says: `/* Deal with special cases: not implemented. */`

2. **It does NOT pre-check orientation or winding.** The reference assumes the polygons are given CCW (PostScript convention) but never validates this.

3. **The "parallel and separated" early `exit(EXIT_SUCCESS)` is real** — it's part of the original algorithm. The reference `exit`s when it detects a clearly-disjoint case. Our port `return {}`s instead.

4. **The `inflag == Unknown && first_point` bail-out is OUR ADDITION, not O'Rourke's.** Look at the reference: it never tests `point_in_convex_poly` — it just emits a comment and stops. The `Pin[0] inside Q` / `Qin[0] inside P` containment check in our port is a custom addition that **assumes CCW winding**.

5. **The "shared edge" detection is also ours.** O'Rourke just calls `PrintSharedSeg` and exits.

6. **The reference does NOT take a convex hull of the output.** It outputs vertices in the order they're found, which is correct for O'Rourke's algorithm because every vertex of the output polygon is either (a) on the boundary of P ∩ Q and is one of the original vertices, or (b) is an intersection of P and Q boundaries. The O'Rourke algorithm produces the convex hull of these *implicitly* because the loop visits the boundary of the intersection polygon in order.

So my "point_in_convex_poly" bug analysis is partially wrong. Let me re-check.

## Bug 1: `point_in_convex_poly` is OURS, not O'Rourke's

Looking at our code at [simplify.cpp:594-601](simplify.cpp):

```cpp
if (inflag == InFlag::Unknown && first_point) {
    // Boundaries do not cross: P is inside Q, or Q is inside P, or they
    // touch at a single point.  Detect containment by sampling one
    // vertex of P.
    if (point_in_convex_poly(Pin[0], Qin)) return Pin;
    if (point_in_convex_poly(Qin[0], Pin)) return Qin;
    return {};
}
```

The reference algorithm has *no such code*. The reference would just exit with empty output. **So when the boundaries don't cross, the reference returns `{}`.** Our port returns `Pin` or `Qin` if either is contained — this is an *enhancement* that we wrote to make the simplify pipeline handle the "P inside G" case.

And yes, `point_in_convex_poly` assumes CCW. But more fundamentally, **the O'Rourke loop should handle containment correctly** if the algorithm were implemented faithfully: when P is entirely inside Q, the loop should detect this through the `inflag` becoming `Pin` and just output the P vertices in order. Let me check…

Looking at the reference, when P is inside Q and edges don't cross:
- `cross` is `area_sign(A, B) = area_sign(Origin, A, B)`. A is the edge of P, B is the edge of Q.
- For a polygon pair where P is strictly inside Q, the edges might not cross but the algorithm needs the right `cross` and `aHB`/`bHA` to advance correctly.
- The reference **doesn't actually handle the containment case** — it just prints the message and exits. The O'Rourke textbook has a separate code path / notes that this is a special case the user must handle.

So strictly speaking, **O'Rourke's published code as written doesn't handle containment**. The textbook discusses it but the reference C code says "not implemented". Our port added the point-in-poly check as a workaround.

## Bug 2: Our port diverges from reference in *advance* logic

Look at the reference `ConvexIntersect` carefully — the advance rules:
The `advance` matches the reference. Let me check the loop body now:

I see the divergence clearly now. Compare to the reference:

| | Reference | Our port |
|---|---|---|
| Output the intersection point | In `InOut()` (called when code=='1' or 'v') | Also at line 551 — same as ref |
| Print + `moveto` only on first | Reference prints p0 in `InOut` only on first call (line `if ( inflag == Unknown && FirstPoint )` in `InOut`) | We do it here, lines 546-550 — same as ref |
| `if FirstPoint` then close lineto | After loop, reference does `if (!FirstPoint) lineto p0` | We do `finish(!first_point)` — same as ref |
| Bail-out on `inflag == Unknown` | Reference just prints message, exits with empty | We added point-in-convex-poly check |

So **the loop body is correct.** The only O'Rourke-faithful differences are:
- We `return {}` instead of `exit` (correct port).
- We added a containment check (an extension, not a bug per se).
- We added a "shared edge" special case (an extension).

## What about the O'Rourke reference C code — what bugs does it have?

The reference C code has its own issues, but those are **the reference's issues, not ours**:

1. **No containment handling.** Reference exits empty when boundaries don't cross. Ours handles containment — so we're *better* than the reference in that one regard (modulo the winding issue).
2. **The `SharedSeg` `exit(EXIT_SUCCESS)`**: reference exits the program on first detection. We `break` and handle. So ours is also more robust.

So my "the algorithm is wrong" framing is too strong. **Our port is more correct than the reference for the containment case.** The bugs are in the *extensions* we added (point-in-convex-poly winding assumption, shared-edge handling).

## Re-checking the test failures against this

Let me look at `[edge_overlap_opposite]` again:
- P = square [-1,-1, 1,-1, 1,1, -1,1] = **CCW**
- Q = square [1,-1, -1,-1, -1,1, 1,1] = **CW** (reversed)

These are the same square but Q is wound CW. Both algorithms return:
- O'Rourke: 2 vertices (degenerate)
- CGAL: 4 vertices (full square)

So O'Rourke is failing on **a CW polygon**. The reference assumes CCW. **Our port matches the reference** in assuming CCW — it's the same bug. The `point_in_convex_poly` extension compounds it for the containment case.

The question is: **why does the main loop fail on CW polygons at all?** The main loop only uses orientation to decide which edge to advance. With a CW polygon, `aHB` and `bHA` signs flip. The reference's "rotate toward in" rule becomes "rotate toward out", so the algorithm walks the wrong way around and never finds the crossings.

**This is a real bug in the reference, and we inherited it.** The fix is winding-agnostic: compute the polygon's signed area once at the start, and if negative, reverse the vertex order (or flip the orientation predicate's sign).

## Re-checking the 3 "empty but should be non-empty" cases

`[rand_n4_m32_r0]`, `[rand_n32_m4_r2]`, `[rand_n128_m128_r2]` all return 0 from O'Rourke but have non-empty intersections per CGAL. **Both algorithms use the same vertex coordinates** (from the random generator). The polygons are CCW by construction (sort by atan2 + convex_hull_2). So this isn't a winding issue.

The O'Rourke main loop, in these cases, **exits with `inflag == Unknown && first_point == true`**. That means **the loop's main body never found a single `code == '1' || code == 'v'`**. This can happen if:
- The two polygons *truly have no edge intersections* but **they overlap** (one is contained in the other, or they share a single tangent point, or…)

For `[rand_n4_m32_r0]`, the test output showed CGAL found a 6-vertex intersection, area 1943. If the polygons are non-touching, the intersection polygon has 6 vertices, all of which are intersections of P and Q edges. Yet O'Rourke finds none. That can ONLY mean **O'Rourke exited early via the "parallel and separated" branch** (line 564-566), which is a real reference bug.

Let me verify: this is an early `return {}` based on a condition that the reference C code has at the **same place** in its loop. The reference's `exit(EXIT_SUCCESS)` there is also a bug — it's an early-exit that fires when `cross == 0 && aHB < 0 && bHA < 0`, meaning the *current* pair of edges is parallel with the polygons on opposite sides. **But other edges of the same polygons might cross.** The reference (and our port) gives up on the entire intersection just because the current edge pair looks parallel.

This is a real bug in the reference algorithm as published. The correct behavior is to *advance* past the parallel pair and try the next edge, not to declare disjointness. **Our port faithfully reproduces this reference bug.**

## So the corrected bug list

| # | Source | Severity | Description | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Reference (faithfully ported) | High | "Parallel and separated" early `exit`/`return {}` (line 564-566). Wrong: only the current edge pair is parallel, not the polygons. | Remove the early return; let the loop continue. |
| 2 | Reference (faithfully ported) | High | Algorithm assumes CCW winding; fails on CW polygons. | Reverse CW polygons before processing. |
| 3 | Our extension | Medium | `point_in_convex_poly` bail-out (lines 496-504, 594-601) is winding-sensitive. | Make it winding-agnostic (signed-area test). |
| 4 | Our extension | Low | `shared_edge` handling may have edge cases. | Verify by testing. |
| 5 | Algorithmic | Low | Vertex-on-edge handling in `between` / `seg_seg_int` — `triangle_intersects_square` missing one vertex. | Trace the specific failure. |

Bug 1 is the root cause of all three "empty but should be non-empty" cases. Bug 2 is the root cause of `edge_overlap_opposite` and any CW-polygon failure. Bug 3 is a secondary issue with our extension. Bug 5 is the `triangle_intersects_square` mismatch.

## The fix plan (now grounded in the reference)

Given the reference, the minimal fix that makes us both correct AND faithful to O'Rourke is:

1. **Remove the "parallel and separated" early return** (line 564-566). This is a real bug in the published reference and we're inheriting it. Removing it lets the loop continue and find real crossings.

2. **Normalize winding at the top of `convex_intersect`**: compute the signed area, and if negative, reverse the vertex vector. Apply the same to `Pin` and `Qin`. This makes the main loop winding-agnostic.

3. **For `point_in_convex_poly`**: same winding-agnostic fix, or just rely on (2) so the input is always CCW.

4. **Final pass**: `CGAL::convex_hull_2(out)` to absorb spurious collinear vertices — this is what the canonical mode does and what the O'Rourke textbook says is fine (the convex hull of the output equals the output for the O'Rourke algorithm, but defensively applying it can't hurt).

**Confirmed.** The "parallel and separated" early return is the bug:

- ORIGINAL (current code, with early return at line 564-566): **0 vertices** — wrong.
- FIXED (early return removed): **10 vertices** — finds the intersection.

The reason this fires: the long thin triangle has a long edge (0,-0.1)→(100,0) that is approximately *parallel* to one of the rectangle's edges when sampled as the first edge pair, and the polygons are on the "separated" sides. The reference algorithm and our port both bail out, but the polygons actually overlap. Removing the early return lets the loop continue and find the actual intersections.

(The 10-vertex output of the FIXED version is also wrong — it has duplicates and runs twice around. But that's a *different* bug: the loop needs to terminate correctly when `cross == 0` for one pair, and the `aa < 2n`/`ba < 2m` guards go around twice. After removing the early return, we also need to be careful about the collinear case. Let me think about this more carefully.)

## Now: the right fix

The "parallel and separated" early return is not strictly necessary if we:

1. Remove the early `return {}`.
2. Add an early-termination check on `aa >= 2n` and `ba >= 2m` (already in the loop condition).
3.
